Do not answer the questions or recommend a plan.

The cooperative has operated a neighborhood laundromat for six years in a ground-floor storefront near the bus depot. It has 38 member households and six paid staff members, including a shift coordinator and a part-time bookkeeper. Members buy an annual share and can attend monthly meetings; staff handle the daily wash-and-fold service, machine maintenance, and customer questions. The shop has 14 washers and 12 dryers, two of which are currently out of service. It also has a small folding area, a counter for detergent sales, and a narrow back room used for staff breaks and storing supplies.

The cooperative’s lease renewal is due in five months. The landlord has offered a three-year extension, but the proposed rent is 11 percent higher than the current rate. The treasurer says the reserve fund could cover several months of rent but has fallen since the cooperative replaced its water heater last winter. At the last meeting, one member said, “I want us to stay here, but I don’t want us to agree to a rent we can’t carry.” Another member replied that moving could mean losing regular customers who walk from nearby apartment buildings. No lease decision has been made, and members have not yet discussed whether to ask the landlord about different terms.

Operating costs have changed unevenly. The water and gas bills rose during the coldest months, while detergent sales were lower than expected in early spring. Wash-and-fold orders are busiest on Fridays and Saturdays, but weekday afternoons can be quiet. Staff say the two broken dryers make weekend queues longer and leave less time for folding orders. A repair technician has estimated that one dryer needs a replacement motor; the other needs a diagnosis before the cost is known. The bookkeeper has not put both repairs into a single estimate because there is not yet a confirmed price for the second machine.

Members have raised several questions about access and services. Some older customers have asked whether the shop could offer help carrying laundry from the sidewalk, while staff are concerned about adding a task without enough coverage during busy shifts. A nearby family shelter has asked about a discounted weekly laundry arrangement, but the cooperative has not discussed what volume it could handle. A member who uses a wheelchair noted that the entrance threshold is difficult to cross, especially when the folding area is crowded. The doorway was mentioned at a meeting last year, but no measurements or contractor estimate were collected. Keep these items as questions for discussion rather than assuming the cooperative has agreed to make changes.

There are also differences of opinion about member participation. A few members attend almost every monthly meeting, while many others have not attended this year. One member suggested holding a meeting on a Saturday morning; another worried that weekend meetings would conflict with the busiest shop hours. The coordinator has proposed a short written update between meetings, but some members prefer face-to-face conversation and want to know who would prepare the update. The cooperative does not have a communications committee, and no one has volunteered to lead one.

we also have a midweek easy run on tuesdays, leaving at 6:15 pm from the same steps. usual distance is roughly 4 kilometres, though people sometimes stop earlier if they need to. it is an easy conversational pace and nobody has to keep up with the quickest person. one of the regulars, imani, said, “i like that we can talk the whole way and still call it a run.” we need to make it clear this is a group run, not individual coaching or a guaranteed training plan. if heavy rain or a safety issue means a run has to change, organizers will post an update in the club's public notice channel by 5:30 pm that day. no cancellation is currently listed. please don't turn that into a claim that weather will be clear.

there are 18 clocks in the room at the moment. five are wall clocks, four mantel clocks, three longcase clocks, and the rest are small travel or desk clocks. two of the longcases are not running; one has a cracked glass panel and a label that says “please don't wind.” don't tell us to test it. the other stops after about twenty minutes, but Malik hasn't looked inside yet. the wall clock with the blue painted face came from Jo's aunt and we have no paperwork for it. we do have a receipt for the small brass carriage clock, but the date on it is smudged. please include a sensible way to keep track of these differences without pretending we know dates, makers, or values.

we're trying to sort out what visitors can see, and how to keep the room safe while we do that. the narrow aisle by the tall case is about 70 centimetres across, and the side door opens into it; that's the exit visitors use. there's a low radiator under the front window and a box of old pendulums currently sits on the floor beside it. the ceiling lights flicker sometimes, especially when the kettle is on, and the only socket near the display bench is loose. we have a folding table, two lamps, three paper signs, and a small lockable cabinet, but no display stands. don't assume we can buy much. ask us to get the electrical issue checked, but don't tell us to repair wiring ourselves. I'd like the plan to say how the clocks, tools, and visitor route might be arranged before the open afternoon.

we also need a basic routine for the clocks, but we don't have a conservator and shouldn't take anything apart just to make it look busy. Jo can clean the outside cases with a dry cloth, and Malik is comfortable checking whether a clock is already running, but neither of them is trained to oil or adjust a movement. one volunteer, Priya, has offered to contact a local horologist; we don't know whether they can visit or what they charge. please include what we can safely record in the meantime, how to label anything that shouldn't be touched, and what questions to ask the horologist without assuming they'll agree to do the work.

our records are spread across a notebook, two phone photo folders, and a spreadsheet that was last updated in January. the notebook has a few handwritten entries like “runs well” with no date or initials. photos often show the clock but not its back, label, or condition. we can probably spend one Tuesday making a shared list, but not a whole day. I want a record that volunteers can update after a visit, with a clear difference between something observed and something we were told. include a simple way to note an uncertain detail and who entered it, and don't suggest throwing away the old notes or changing the spreadsheet before we've checked what's already there.

for the visitors, we want a short explanation of how a mechanical clock works, but nobody has agreed to give a talk. Jo might welcome people and Malik may be able to demonstrate winding a clock that is cleared for it, though he doesn't want that presented as a promise. one visitor last month asked, “Is the ticking meant to sound uneven?” We didn't know which clock they meant. please make the plan leave room for questions and avoid claiming every clock is working or original. we have a magnifying glass, a few old trade catalogues, and a printed map showing where some of the clocks were collected; the map has two pencil marks we can't identify.

we need to check permissions too. the shop is rented, the landlord allows the regular Saturday opening, and we haven't asked about extra chairs, a banner on the pavement, or use of the back room. the fire instructions are in a folder by the front desk, but I don't know when someone last reviewed them. there's a first aid kit in the kitchen and a sign-in sheet for volunteers, not for visitors. please don't state that the open afternoon is approved, or assume we can put anything outside. say who could ask the landlord and what should be confirmed before we advertise a date. the likely date is the 14th, but we haven't said which month in the poster draft.

could you make this a practical plan with a week-by-week sequence for eight weeks, but keep the end date conditional on the landlord's answer. Include a short numbered section for the things that need a decision or confirmation, and separate immediate tasks from things that depend on expert advice. We have about £120 available, but that may need to cover printing and refreshments as well as supplies; don't assign the whole amount to clock materials. Give tasks an owner only where I've named someone or where you can phrase it as a volunteer role, and make clear that these are suggestions rather than agreed commitments. Don't calculate a value for any clock or add new staff, equipment, historical facts, repairs, or assurances. End with a brief list of open questions we should resolve at our next Tuesday meeting, including anything you can't infer from this request.","response":"Create a practical, realistic eight-week plan for the volunteer-run antique clock room in the old Mercer Street print shop. The group has six volunteers, but usually only Jo, Malik, and the requester attend on Tuesdays. The room opens to visitors two Saturdays a month. A larger open afternoon is being considered for the 14th, but the landlord has not confirmed use of the back room, and the poster draft does not specify the month. Keep the event date and plan conditional where necessary. Distinguish actions that can begin now from decisions or permissions that are still needed. Treat suggested tasks as suggestions, not agreed commitments, and assign named owners only to people identified below; otherwise use a volunteer role.

### 1. Eight-week sequence
Provide a week-by-week sequence that fits the group’s limited time, including the possibility of spending one Tuesday on a shared records list. Show how the plan would prepare the room and visitors’ route before the possible open afternoon. Separate immediate tasks from tasks that depend on the landlord, electrical checks, or expert advice. Do not assume the event is approved.

### 2. Clocks, records, and safe care
There are 18 clocks: five wall clocks, four mantel clocks, three longcase clocks, and six small travel or desk clocks. One longcase has cracked glass and a label reading “please don't wind”; do not recommend testing or winding it. The other stops after about twenty minutes; Malik has not inspected its interior. Jo’s aunt owned the wall clock with the blue painted face, and there is no paperwork for it. There is a receipt for the small brass carriage clock, but its date is smudged. Do not invent dates, makers, values, or other history.

Recommend a simple record that volunteers can update after a visit and that distinguishes direct observations from information reported by others. Include a way to record uncertain details and who entered them. Existing records are in a notebook, two phone photo folders, and a spreadsheet last updated in January. Some notebook entries, such as “runs well,” lack dates and initials; many photos do not show the clock’s back, label, or condition. The group may be able to spend one Tuesday making a shared list, but not a whole day. Do not recommend discarding old notes or changing the spreadsheet before checking what is already there.

Suggest safe interim observations and labels for clocks that should not be touched. Jo can dust exterior cases with a dry cloth; Malik is comfortable checking whether a clock is already running. Neither is trained to oil or adjust a movement. Priya has offered to contact a local horologist, but availability and cost are unknown. Identify questions to ask the horologist without assuming they will visit or do the work. Do not advise taking clocks apart merely to demonstrate activity.

### 3. Room setup and visitor experience
Plan for a safe visitor route and arrangement of clocks, tools, and visitor materials before the possible event. The aisle beside the tall case is about 70 centimetres wide; the side door opens into that aisle and is the visitors’ exit. A low radiator is under the front window, with a box of old pendulums on the floor beside it. The ceiling lights sometimes flicker, especially when the kettle is on, and the socket near the display bench is loose. Ask the group to have the electrical issue checked; do not suggest that volunteers repair wiring. Available items are a folding table, two lamps, three paper signs, and a small lockable cabinet. There are no display stands, and the budget is limited, so do not assume substantial purchases.

Allow for a short explanation of how a mechanical clock works, but do not assume anyone has agreed to give a talk. Jo might welcome visitors. Malik may be able to demonstrate winding a clock that has been cleared for it, but does not want this treated as a promise. Make room for visitor questions, including the question asked last month: “Is the ticking meant to sound uneven?” The visitor did not identify which clock they meant. Avoid claiming that all clocks work or are original. The room has a magnifying glass, several old trade catalogues, and a printed map showing where some clocks were collected; two pencil marks on the map are unidentified.

### 4. Permissions, budget, and confirmations
The shop is rented. The landlord permits the regular Saturday openings, but nobody has asked about extra chairs, a pavement banner, or using the back room. The requester can ask about the landlord contact, but do not state that the event or any of these arrangements is approved. Identify what must be confirmed before advertising a date, including the month. Fire instructions are in a folder by the front desk, but their last review date is unknown. There is a first aid kit in the kitchen and a volunteer sign-in sheet, but no visitor sign-in sheet; do not infer additional requirements or claim these arrangements have been reviewed.

The available budget is about £120 and may also need to cover printing and refreshments. Do not allocate all of it to clock materials. Keep suggested spending modest and identify costs that need checking rather than assuming prices.

End with a brief open-questions list for the next Tuesday meeting. Include unresolved details that cannot be inferred from this request, and use a short numbered section to identify decisions or confirmations needed. Do not add staff, equipment, historical facts, repairs, clock values, approvals, or assurances."}

lowercase","response":"Organize this request into a clear prompt for generating useful discussion questions about learning sign language. Keep the setting and constraints below; do not answer the prompt by writing the questions.

The discussion is part of a fictional episode set in an evening beginner American Sign Language (ASL) class at a neighborhood community center. Eight adults attend, and the class has been meeting for six weeks. They are learning together, not training to become interpreters. The instructor, Lena Ortiz, is Deaf and has taught community classes for several years. The episode focuses on the learners’ experiences and the choices they make as beginners, rather than presenting Lena as someone who should speak for every Deaf person. The discussion will take place after class, with Lena and the learners in the room. A few learners may speak more than others, so the questions should make it easy for everyone to participate without putting anyone on the spot.

The learners have varied reasons for enrolling. One wants to communicate more easily with a Deaf cousin; another has a Deaf coworker but does not want to assume what that coworker prefers. Two learners are interested in Deaf culture, while one signed up because the class fit their schedule and is still figuring out their goals. Several have tried learning from videos or apps before, but none of them has studied ASL formally. They are beginning with fingerspelling, greetings, introductions, and everyday phrases. They sometimes mix up handshapes or forget to look at the signer’s face, and they are learning that facial expression and movement can carry grammatical meaning. Do not assume that all the learners have the same motivation, confidence, or prior experience.

The class meets once a week for ninety minutes. Lena demonstrates signs, gives learners time to practice in pairs, and invites them to ask for clarification. She has reminded the class that signs can vary by region and person, and that learners should not treat one classroom example as the only possible form. At the last meeting, one student asked how to tell when a sign was unfamiliar rather than simply missed. Lena said, “It’s okay to ask me to slow down or show it again.” Another learner wondered whether it was rude to use a phone dictionary during practice. The class did not settle every question, and the discussion questions should leave room for different experiences rather than imply there is one universal answer.

The aim is to help the eight learners talk about what learning feels like in practice: what has been encouraging, what has been awkward, what they notice when they watch someone sign, and how they respond when communication breaks down. Invite reflection on practice habits, remembering signs between weekly meetings, and learning with other people rather than only through an app. Include room to discuss how learners can ask someone about communication preferences respectfully, without making a Deaf person responsible for teaching them or representing a whole community. The questions should be open-ended, concrete, and suitable for a mixed group of beginners. They should not sound like a quiz about vocabulary or test whether someone is a “good” learner.

Please make the discussion useful even if a participant is shy or has not yet had a major breakthrough. Ask about small moments, such as remembering a greeting, noticing a facial expression, or needing a sign repeated. It may be helpful to include a question about what a learner does when they feel embarrassed after making a mistake, but do not assume that everyone feels embarrassed. Some learners may prefer to listen before answering. Avoid questions that require anyone to disclose a family member’s private information, explain a personal relationship, or demonstrate a sign in front of the group. A question can invite people to share an example if they want to, but it should not demand one.

The discussion should be grounded in this particular class and still be relevant to adults learning a sign language elsewhere. Do not turn it into a general guide to ASL, an argument about which learning resource is best, or a lesson in Deaf culture. It is fine to ask how the learners decide what to practice next, what they find useful in class versus videos or apps, and what they still wonder about. Keep questions respectful about Deaf people and avoid portraying sign language as a collection of gestures or as a quick fix for communication. If a question touches on variation, frame it as something learners are noticing and learning about, not a problem that needs to be corrected.

Maybe group the discussion into a few stages so it can start lightly and move toward reflection without feeling like an interview. The first part could help people check in about the six weeks of class. A middle part could explore practice, visual attention, asking for repetition, and the different reasons people are learning. A later part might look ahead to what learners want to try next and what support would help them keep going. The group has about twenty-five minutes, so the questions should be selective rather than exhaustive. Do not make a full lesson plan or add timing instructions for every question.

Please use a numbered section in the prompt to make the main areas of inquiry easy to scan. Those areas can include starting motivations, confidence and mistakes, practice between classes, visual communication, respectful ways to ask about preferences, and next steps. These are topic areas for questions, not claims that everyone has had the same experience. The resulting questions should vary in focus rather than asking the same thing in slightly different words. Keep wording conversational and clear enough to read aloud in a community-center discussion. Avoid jargon, leading questions, and language that suggests there is a single correct path for learning ASL.

The result should be a manageable set of discussion questions for this episode, not a script, summary, or list of answers. Give the facilitator a few options to choose from, since twenty-five minutes may not allow every question to be used. Keep Lena and the learners’ circumstances as described, retain the possibility that people have different experiences, and do not add new participants, class events, or conclusions about how the group feels. The questions should support a thoughtful conversation about learning ASL as beginners while leaving participants free to pass or respond in their own way.","reasoning":null}

here are the notes, a bit jumbled because they came from different places. mara is an adult beginner studying american sign language (asl) at a free tuesday evening class in the east branch public library in tacoma. the class starts at 6:30 and usually has eight learners. lena ortiz teaches it. mara signed up because a colleague’s family uses asl at home, but she said she didn’t want to treat one class as preparation for speaking for that family. the first meeting was february 6. lena explained that the class was for beginners and that people could ask questions or pass during practice. mara is right-handed. that night they practiced handshapes, exchanging names, and fingerspelling. she wrote that she could fingerspell her own name slowly but had to pause to recognize unfamiliar names.

february 13 was mostly fingerspelling and short introductions. lena asked learners to look at the signer rather than down at their own hands. mara wrote, “I can recognize it when I see it, but my hands get ahead of my eyes.” she also noted that she tended to watch individual fingers and miss a change in the other person’s expression. one classmate, eli, practiced names with her after class for about ten minutes. the notes don’t say that either learner was assigned a name sign. on february 20 the group worked on basic vocabulary for family and everyday routines, then watched a short signed clip twice. lena paused the second viewing to point out that facial expression and movement can affect meaning. mara said she was surprised that watching the whole person felt harder than memorizing a handshape.

her practice log from the next two weeks says she tried to practice at home for about twelve minutes on four evenings, using the class handout and a mirror. she reviewed the alphabet and the family words, then filmed herself signing three short introductions on her phone. she deleted one recording because she had turned her body away from the camera. she wrote that the mirror helped her notice her hands, but it also made her keep looking away from the video she was copying. one evening she skipped practice because she was tired after work; she did not describe this as a setback, just a missed session. she brought the phone clip to class the next tuesday and asked lena whether her hands were too low in the frame. lena suggested positioning the phone farther back, and mara wrote that this made it easier to see her arms and face together.

on march 5, the class practiced questions and short exchanges in pairs. mara’s note says she could follow the first exchange when it was slow, but lost track when her partner added a new detail. she started to answer before the other person finished, then stopped and asked them to repeat it. lena reminded the group to leave time for the other person to finish signing. mara called that useful, though she said she still felt awkward about waiting. the class had a guest visitor, jo, a deaf community member who talked about everyday communication and answered questions. one note from mara says jo asked people to get attention in a visible way and not to grab someone. another says jo encouraged learners to ask a person how they prefer to communicate instead of assuming. mara wrote down, “please don't guess my name sign; ask me first.” this is quoted from jo, not a name-sign decision about mara.

on march 12, mara went with eli to a casual asl meetup at a community center. her notes say they mostly watched and introduced themselves to two people, and she understood a few familiar signs but missed much of a fast group conversation. she didn’t claim that the meetup was a test or that anyone evaluated her. she wrote that it was helpful to see people take turns and use their faces, and that she was unsure when to join in. the following tuesday in class, she mentioned the meetup and asked lena how beginners can signal that they want a slower repeat. lena modeled asking for repetition and slowing down, but mara’s notes don’t say she used those phrases at the meetup.

a couple of other details are scattered in the margins: the library handout had drawings of handshapes and arrows for movement; the class did not use a textbook. learners were asked to practice with each other only when both people wanted to. mara says she likes the small class because she can ask a question without interrupting a lecture, but she also worries about taking too long when it is her turn. by the end of these notes, she can fingerspell familiar names more steadily and recognize some class vocabulary, but she still struggles to follow unfamiliar or fast signing. that’s where the material stops. for the summary, please keep that limited endpoint clear and don’t turn it into a success story or a judgment of her ability.

can you help me turn this into a clear prompt for writing a practical camera-trap image review protocol? it’s for a small volunteer team at alder reach reserve, not a research paper and not a summary of what the cameras found. the reserve covers about 2,400 hectares, with reedbed, wet meadow, and willow scrub. we ran twelve cameras from 4 september to 16 october 2025, mostly beside animal paths, two culverts, and the edges of the boardwalks. i’m not sure every unit recorded for the full period, so don’t say they all did.

we used browning strike force pro xd and reconyx hyperfire 2 cameras. the cards have been copied to a shared drive folder called AR_2025_AUTUMN. three volunteers and one ranger will review the files. they have basic wildlife familiarity but haven’t used a consistent labeling system before. the images are jpegs, with a few short avi clips mixed in; we don’t yet know how many files are blank or unusable. the protocol should be understandable to someone opening the folder for the first time, and it should explain the review steps in order rather than assume the reader knows our setup.

for each usable image or clip, reviewers need to record the camera id, file name, date and time as shown (with the offset note if there is one), whether an animal is visible, the best supported species label, number of visible animals when countable, and a short behavior note. also include an image-quality field with choices such as clear, partly obscured, too dark, or unusable, and a confidence field for the identification. i’d like the instructions to make it okay to use “unknown” or a broader group label when the picture doesn’t support a species-level call. don’t ask volunteers to guess sex or age; record those only if clearly visible, and otherwise leave them unrecorded.

we need a rule for grouping repeated pictures into events. please use a 30-minute gap between detections of the same species at the same camera as the default boundary for separate events. if there is clear evidence in the pictures that a different individual has appeared sooner, reviewers can note that in the behavior or comments field, but the protocol shouldn’t make them invent individual identities. people in a frame aren’t wildlife detections. if a person is captured, tell reviewers not to copy that image into slides or ordinary reports and to flag it to the ranger for restricted handling; we haven’t chosen a separate retention process yet.

one ranger said, “if you can’t tell what it is, a careful unknown is better than a confident guess.” i want that idea worked into the guidance without making it sound like every uncertain picture is worthless. reviewers should be able to leave a short note when two people disagree, and the ranger should make the final label decision for those cases. don’t claim we already have agreement or a quality-control result. mention that the protocol is for reviewing this autumn folder, not for changing camera placement, planning a new survey, or estimating animal populations.

could you have the prompt request these parts, in a useful order?
1. a short purpose and scope, including the dates and reserve setting
2. file-opening and source-file handling steps
3. the fields reviewers should enter, with plain-language definitions
4. the image, clip, timestamp, uncertainty, and event rules
5. what to do with people in images and with disagreements
6. a brief closing checklist before a reviewer marks a camera folder complete

please keep the instructions grounded in the details here. there isn’t a supplied species list, spreadsheet template, camera map, complete clock record, or agreed privacy-retention policy, so don’t pretend those exist or fill them in. the result should ask for a usable protocol with clearly marked limits, not a made-up analysis of detections and not a general wildlife-camera essay. use straightforward language, and make it suitable to share with the volunteers and ranger as a draft for this specific review.","response":"Write a practical, clearly organized camera-trap image review protocol for the volunteer team and ranger at Alder Reach Reserve. The protocol is for reviewing the existing autumn image folder only; it is not a research paper, a summary of camera findings, a population estimate, a plan for a new survey, or advice on changing camera placement. Use straightforward language and explain the steps in order for reviewers who have basic wildlife familiarity but have not used a consistent labeling system.

## Context and scope

The reserve covers about 2,400 hectares and includes reedbed, wet meadow, and willow scrub. Twelve cameras were run from 4 September to 16 October 2025, mostly beside animal paths, two culverts, and boardwalk edges. Do not state or imply that every camera recorded throughout the full period; it is not known whether all units did. The cameras were Browning Strike Force Pro XD and Reconyx HyperFire 2 models. Three volunteers and one ranger will review the files in the shared-drive folder `AR_2025_AUTUMN`.

## File handling

Explain how a reviewer should open and work through the folder structure, which is arranged by camera ID, date received, and card number. Preserve original filenames and do not edit or delete source files. The files are JPEG images, with a few short AVI clips mixed in. The number of blank or unusable files is not yet known. Include a clear way to handle those files as part of the review without assuming a count or result.

Camera clocks may not match actual time. Some cameras have offset notes and others do not, and there is no complete clock-check record. Tell reviewers to use a documented offset only when one is available, and otherwise mark the time as uncertain. Do not silently convert timestamps or imply that they are exact.

## Review fields

For each usable image or clip, instruct reviewers to record:
- Camera ID and original filename.
- Date and time as shown, with a documented offset note when available.
- Whether an animal is visible.
- The best-supported species label, using “unknown” or a broader group label when the image does not support a species-level identification.
- Number of visible animals, when countable.
- A short behavior note.
- Image quality, using choices such as clear, partly obscured, too dark, or unusable.
- Identification confidence.

Do not ask reviewers to guess an animal’s sex or age. Record either only when clearly visible; otherwise leave it unrecorded. Define the fields in plain language so reviewers can apply them consistently.

## Images, events, and uncertainty

Cover both JPEG images and AVI clips. Use a 30-minute gap between detections of the same species at the same camera as the default boundary for separate events. If pictures provide clear evidence that a different individual appeared sooner, reviewers may note that in the behavior or comments field. Do not ask them to invent or assign individual identities.

Include the guidance: “If you can’t tell what it is, a careful unknown is better than a confident guess.” Make clear that uncertainty does not make every image worthless. Allow reviewers to add a short note when they disagree about a label, and direct the ranger to make the final label decision in those cases. Do not claim that reviewers already agree or that quality control has produced a result.

People in a frame are not wildlife detections. If a person is captured, reviewers should not copy the image into slides or ordinary reports and should flag it to the ranger for restricted handling. A separate retention process has not been chosen, so do not invent one.

## Requested sections

Organize the protocol to include, in a useful order:
1. A short purpose and scope that gives the dates and reserve setting.
2. File-opening and source-file handling steps.
3. The review fields and plain-language definitions.
4. Rules for images, clips, timestamps, uncertainty, and events.
5. Instructions for handling images of people and reviewer disagreements.
6. A brief closing checklist for marking a camera folder complete.

Keep the protocol grounded in the information above. No species list, spreadsheet template, camera map, complete clock record, or agreed privacy-retention policy has been supplied; do not imply that any of these exists or fill in missing information.
